claim: Myelin increases the conduction velocity of action potentials in long-axon connections.
source: Myelination is well known to be important in increasing the speed of action potential propagation in long-axon connections (Waxman and Bennett, 1972; Moore et al., 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to Waxman and Bennett, 1972 and Moore et al., 1978

claim: Myelin increases the metabolic efficiency of action potentials.
source: Because myelin increases the conduction velocity of action potentials and reduces their metabolic cost (Nave, 2010; but see Harris and Attwell, 2012), it has traditionally been viewed as 'wire insulation' for long-range neural projections.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nave, 2010, with a caveat from Harris and Attwell, 2012

claim: Adult-born oligodendrocytes contribute new myelin to axons in an ongoing fashion.
source: For example, adult-born oligodendrocytes (the myelin-producing cells of the CNS) contribute new myelin to axons in an ongoing fashion (Young et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Young et al., 2013

claim: Increased neuronal activity results in more myelination.
source: increased neuronal activity results in more myelination (Gibson et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gibson et al., 2014

claim: Myelin remodeling in the CNS is required for motor skill acquisition.
source: myelin remodeling in the CNS is required for motor skill acquisition (McKenzie et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to McKenzie et al., 2014

claim: Myelin supplies ensheathed axons with lactate via the monocarboxylate transporter MCT1.
source: Myelin also supplies ensheathed axons with lactate via the monocarboxylate transporter MCT1, possibly playing an important energetic support role in the CNS (Rinholm et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Morrison et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rinholm et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Morrison et al., 2013

claim: Excitatory pyramidal neurons in cortex are a main source of long-range myelinated axons connecting the two cortical hemispheres or targeting subcortical structures.
source: Excitatory pyramidal neurons in cortex are known to be a main source of long-range myelinated axons connecting the two cortical hemispheres or targeting subcortical structures.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge without specific citation in this sentence

claim: Local axon collaterals of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons may be myelinated.
source: Foundational EM-based studies of individual Golgi- or dye-filled neurons (Kisvárday et al., 1986; Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Peters and Proskauer, 1980; Tamás et al., 1997) have revealed that the local axon collaterals of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons may also be myelinated.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kisvárday et al., 1986; Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Peters and Proskauer, 1980; Tamás et al., 1997

claim: Golgi labeling of neurons halts where the axon first enters a myelin sheath.
source: Golgi labeling of neurons halts where the axon first enters a myelin sheath (Peters and Proskauer, 1980; DeFelipe et al., 1986; Fairén et al., 1977)
evidence: Supported by citations to Peters and Proskauer, 1980; DeFelipe et al., 1986; Fairén et al., 1977

claim: Myelination of the axons of pyramidal neurons in cortex is distinct from the known myelination patterns in subcortical white matter.
source: Myelin tracing in large EM datasets has revealed that myelination of the axons of pyramidal neurons in cortex is distinct from the known myelination patterns in subcortical white matter, and also differs between cortical layers (Tomassy et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tomassy et al., 2014

claim: About 10–20% of neocortical neurons are inhibitory.
source: About 10–20% of neocortical neurons are inhibitory and some of these neurons may also have myelinated axons.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Inhibitory neurons may have myelinated axons.
source: For example, labeling of individual neocortical neurons during in vivo electrophysiological recording, followed by light-level reconstruction and electron microscopy (EM) of selected sub-arbors, has revealed that inhibitory neurons may be myelinated (DeFelipe et al., 1986; Somogyi et al., 1983; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998; Kisvarday et al., 1987; Thomson et al., 1996; Tamás et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeFelipe et al., 1986; Somogyi et al., 1983; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998; Kisvarday et al., 1987; Thomson et al., 1996; Tamás et al., 1997

claim: Parvalbumin-positive axons may be myelinated.
source: Complementary immunohistochemical studies have shown that parvalbumin-positive (i.e., putative inhibitory [Rudy et al., 2011]) axons may be myelinated (McGee et al., 2005; Chung and Deisseroth, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to McGee et al., 2005; Chung and Deisseroth, 2013

claim: A large fraction of cortical myelin ensheathes axons of inhibitory neurons, specifically parvalbumin-positive basket cells.
source: We find that an unexpectedly large proportion of myelinated axons in cortex arise from a specific subtype of inhibitory neuron: the parvalbumin-positive (PV+) basket cell.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data from both array tomography and volume EM

claim: PV+ axons constitute about half of all myelinated axons in layers 2/3.
source: They constitute about half of all myelinated axons in layers 2/3, and a quarter of myelinated axons in layer 4.
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding of the study

claim: PV+ axons constitute a quarter of myelinated axons in layer 4.
source: They constitute about half of all myelinated axons in layers 2/3, and a quarter of myelinated axons in layer 4.
evidence: This is a primary quantitative finding of the study

claim: Inhibitory myelinated axons in cortical gray matter differ from excitatory myelinated axons in distribution.
source: We also find that the inhibitory myelinated axons in cortical gray matter differ from the excitatory myelinated axons in many respects, such as their structural organization, cytoskeletal content, and myelin protein composition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: Inhibitory myelinated axons in cortical gray matter differ from excitatory myelinated axons in cytoskeletal content.
source: We also find that the inhibitory myelinated axons in cortical gray matter differ from the excitatory myelinated axons in many respects, such as their structural organization, cytoskeletal content, and myelin protein composition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: Inhibitory myelinated axons in cortical gray matter differ from excitatory myelinated axons in myelin protein composition.
source: We also find that the inhibitory myelinated axons in cortical gray matter differ from the excitatory myelinated axons in many respects, such as their structural organization, cytoskeletal content, and myelin protein composition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: Myelin on inhibitory axons is unlikely to meaningfully hasten the arrival of spikes at their pre-synaptic terminals due to the patchy distribution and short path-lengths observed.
source: Myelin on inhibitory axons is unlikely to meaningfully hasten the arrival of spikes at their pre-synaptic terminals, due to the patchy distribution and short path-lengths observed.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural observations from the study

claim: More than 45% of myelinated axons in layers 2/3 contain GABA.
source: Immunostaining for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA reveals that a surprisingly large number of myelinated axons throughout cortex contain GABA, including more than 45% of myelinated axons in layers 2/3 (48.1 ± 3.2%, mean ± standard error, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography experiments

claim: 48.1 ± 3.2% of myelinated axons in layers 2/3 contain GABA.
source: Immunostaining for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA reveals that a surprisingly large number of myelinated axons throughout cortex contain GABA, including more than 45% of myelinated axons in layers 2/3 (48.1 ± 3.2%, mean ± standard error, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a precise quantitative finding from array tomography experiments

claim: GABA myelinated axons are relatively sparse in layers 1 and 6.
source: GABA myelinated axons are relatively sparse in layers 1, 6, and only occasionally seen in subcortical white matter.
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography experiments

claim: GABA myelinated axons are only occasionally seen in subcortical white matter.
source: GABA myelinated axons are relatively sparse in layers 1, 6, and only occasionally seen in subcortical white matter.
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography experiments

claim: 45.9% of myelinated axons in layer 2/3 of mouse visual cortex are inhibitory based on synapse ultrastructure.
source: Of the 231 myelinated 'seeds', 73 were classified as excitatory (31.6%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), 106 as inhibitory (45.9%; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and 52 (22.5%; Figure 2—figure supplement 3) could not be categorized due to an absence of synapses within the volume.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM tracing

claim: 31.6% of myelinated axons in layer 2/3 of mouse visual cortex are excitatory based on synapse ultrastructure.
source: Of the 231 myelinated 'seeds', 73 were classified as excitatory (31.6%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), 106 as inhibitory (45.9%; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and 52 (22.5%; Figure 2—figure supplement 3) could not be categorized due to an absence of synapses within the volume.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM tracing

claim: 22.5% of myelinated axons in layer 2/3 could not be categorized due to an absence of synapses within the volume.
source: Of the 231 myelinated 'seeds', 73 were classified as excitatory (31.6%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), 106 as inhibitory (45.9%; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and 52 (22.5%; Figure 2—figure supplement 3) could not be categorized due to an absence of synapses within the volume.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM tracing

claim: Nearly all GABA myelinated axons (97.9 ± 0.8%) are immunopositive for parvalbumin.
source: Array tomography (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) revealed that nearly all GABA myelinated axons (97.9 ± 0.8%, mean ± st.error from 3 animals) are immunopositive for parvalbumin and therefore originate from PV interneurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography experiments

claim: About half (53 ± 12%) of the myelinated axons in layer 2/3 of somatosensory cortex contain PV in PV-Cre reporter mice.
source: Confocal imaging of 40 μm thick Vibratome slices from these mice immunostained with MBP corroborated the AT findings by showing that about half (53 ± 12%) of the myelinated axons in layer 2/3 of somatosensory cortex contain tdTomato and, therefore, PV (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunohistochemistry experiments in transgenic mice

claim: No myelinated axons containing reporter for VIP could be observed.
source: After careful inspection of selected subareas, no myelinated axons containing reporter for the non-PV cortical interneurons vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP; Figure 4E–G) could be observed.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry experiments in transgenic mice

claim: A small fraction (4.4%) of somatostatin (SOM)-positive myelinated axons were observed.
source: A small fraction (4.4%) of somatostatin (SOM)-positive myelinated axons were observed (Figure 4H–J)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from immunohistochemistry experiments in transgenic mice

claim: The SOM-Cre line used has a small but consistent false-positive expression pattern, wherein up to 10% of Cre-expressing neurons are SOM-negative and PV-positive.
source: however, the transgenic reporter line used was recently found to have a small but consistent false-positive expression pattern, wherein up to 10% of Cre-expressing neurons are SOM-negative and PV-positive when examined by immunohistochemistry (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2013

claim: The postsynaptic targets of inhibitory myelinated axons are consistent with their originating from local axonal arbors of cortical basket cells.
source: The observed distribution of postsynaptic targets of myelinated inhibitory axons was consistent with their originating from local axonal arbors of cortical basket cells, and inconsistent with their arising from either chandelier cells or long-range inhibitory afferents to cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the postsynaptic target analysis from volume EM

claim: Less than 2% of the inhibitory myelinated axons make contacts on axon initial segments.
source: Less than 2% of the inhibitory myelinated axons in our volume electron microscopy dataset were found to make contacts on axon initial segments (Figure 5; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM analysis

claim: The great preponderance (93%) of postsynaptic targets of myelinated inhibitory axons in layer 2/3 of cortex were excitatory.
source: The great preponderance (93%) of postsynaptic targets of myelinated inhibitory axons in layer 2/3 of cortex were excitatory, likewise eliminating the possibility that these axons originated from the arbors of the known parvalbumin-positive long-range inhibitory afferents to cortex, all of which selectively target inhibitory neurons (Freund and Gulyás, 1991; Gritti et al., 2003; Henny and Jones, 2008).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM analysis, with supporting citations

claim: 13% of the postsynaptic targets of the myelinated inhibitory axons were with somata.
source: Consistent with past surveys of basket cell synaptic targets, we found that 13% of the postsynaptic targets of the myelinated inhibitory axons were with somata, 49% were onto excitatory dendritic shafts, and 30% were onto dendritic spines (Figure 6; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM analysis

claim: 49% of the postsynaptic targets of the myelinated inhibitory axons were onto excitatory dendritic shafts.
source: Consistent with past surveys of basket cell synaptic targets, we found that 13% of the postsynaptic targets of the myelinated inhibitory axons were with somata, 49% were onto excitatory dendritic shafts, and 30% were onto dendritic spines (Figure 6; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM analysis

claim: 30% of the postsynaptic targets of the myelinated inhibitory axons were onto dendritic spines.
source: Consistent with past surveys of basket cell synaptic targets, we found that 13% of the postsynaptic targets of the myelinated inhibitory axons were with somata, 49% were onto excitatory dendritic shafts, and 30% were onto dendritic spines (Figure 6; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM analysis

claim: The axon of a parvalbumin interneuron becomes myelinated soon after exiting the cell body (usually within 20–50 μm).
source: Both our volume electron microscopy and array tomography data show that the axon of a parvalbumin interneuron becomes myelinated soon after exiting the cell body (usually within 20–50 μm), consistent with myelination commencing shortly after the axon initial segment.
evidence: This is a finding from both volume EM and array tomography

claim: All of the axonal arbors that were traced back to the cell body (n=8) had a central core of partially myelinated axons from which emerged unmyelinated branches forming numerous synapses.
source: All of the axonal arbors that were traced back to the cell body in our volume EM dataset (n=8) had the same general appearance: a central core of partially myelinated axons (whose unmyelinated stretches rarely made synapses), from which emerged unmyelinated branches forming numerous synapses (Figures 2C, 5A,C).
evidence: This is a finding from volume EM analysis

claim: The nodes of Ranvier of GABA axons are shorter than for non-GABA axons (0.98 ± 0.07 μm vs. 1.51 ± 0.05 μm).
source: Throughout the cortical layers, the nodes of GABA axons were shorter than for non-GABA axons (0.98 ± 0.07 μm vs. 1.51 ± 0.05 μm, mean ± standard error, p<0.0001, n=71 GABA and 209 non-GABA nodes of Ranvier, Mann-Whitney U Test; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: The internodes of GABA axons are shorter than for non-GABA axons (22.54 ± 2.11 μm vs 29.29 ± 2.02 μm).
source: Their internodes, the myelinated portion between two nodes of Ranvier, were also found to be shorter (22.54 ± 2.11 μm vs 29.29 ± 2.02 μm for non-GABA axons, mean ± standard error, p=0.032, n=23 GABA axons and 32 non-GABA axons, Mann-Whitney U Test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: There is no correlation between myelin thickness and axon diameter within mouse cerebral cortex.
source: However, we found no such correlation within mouse cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography analysis that contradicts expectations from PNS studies

claim: The average myelin thickness is 0.13 ± 0.002 μm for both GABA and non-GABA axons.
source: Using a deconvolved array tomography dataset with MBP and GABA immunofluorescence, we found that the average myelin thickness was 0.13 ± 0.002 μm for both GABA and non-GABA axons (mean ± standard error, n=163 GABA and 238 non-GABA axons from layers 4 and 5, p=0.88, Mann-Whitney U Test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: Myelin thickness does not correlate with axon thickness (R=0.008).
source: and it did not correlate with axon thickness (R=0.008; n=163 GABA and 238 non-GABA axons from layers 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: GABA axons are thicker than non-GABA axons (0.54 ± 0.001 μm vs. 0.45 ± 0.001 μm).
source: GABA axons are thicker than non-GABA axons (0.54 ± 0.001 μm vs. 0.45 ± 0.001 μm, n=163 GABA and 238 non-GABA axons, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U Test; and Figure 8A)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: The average g-ratio of GABA axons is higher than non-GABA axons (0.66 ± 0.006 vs. 0.61 ± 0.006).
source: thus their average g-ratio is higher (0.66 ± 0.006 vs. 0.61 ± 0.006, n=163 GABA and 238 non-GABA axons, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U Test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: GABA myelinated axons have almost 20% higher MBP immunofluorescence than non-GABA axons (5263 ± 117 a.u. vs. 4486 ± 63 a.u.).
source: GABA myelinated axons had almost 20% higher MBP immunofluorescence (5263 ± 117 a.u. vs. 4486 ± 63 a.u., mean ± standard error, n=254 GABA axons and 489 non-GABA, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U Test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: The average PLP immunofluorescence is very similar in both GABA and non-GABA axons (2229 ± 60 a.u. vs 2282 ± 40 a.u.).
source: While the average PLP immunofluorescence was very similar in both types of axons (2229 ± 60 a.u. vs 2282 ± 40 a.u., for GABA and non-GABA axons respectively; mean ± standard error, n=254 GABA axons and 489 non-GABA, p=0.2713, Mann-Whitney U Test, Figure 8D)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: Myelinated GABA axons are rich in neurofilaments and have relatively low microtubule content.
source: Immunostaining for the neurofilament heavy chain and for alpha tubulin revealed that myelinated GABA axons are rich in neurofilaments and have relatively low microtubule content, while the cytoskeleton of myelinated non-GABA axons is dominated by microtubules (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography analysis

claim: The cytoskeleton of myelinated non-GABA axons is dominated by microtubules.
source: Immunostaining for the neurofilament heavy chain and for alpha tubulin revealed that myelinated GABA axons are rich in neurofilaments and have relatively low microtubule content, while the cytoskeleton of myelinated non-GABA axons is dominated by microtubules (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography analysis

claim: GABA myelinated axons contain on average only 66% of the alpha tubulin found in non-GABA myelinated axons.
source: While GABA myelinated axons contain on average only 66% of the alpha tubulin found in non-GABA myelinated axons, they have 86% of the acetylated alpha tubulin content of non-GABA myelinated axons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: GABA myelinated axons have 86% of the acetylated alpha tubulin content of non-GABA myelinated axons.
source: While GABA myelinated axons contain on average only 66% of the alpha tubulin found in non-GABA myelinated axons, they have 86% of the acetylated alpha tubulin content of non-GABA myelinated axons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from array tomography analysis

claim: Both the myelinated and the unmyelinated regions of the GABA axons have higher neurofilament content and lower microtubule content compared to non-GABA axons.
source: First, the cytoskeletal composition of axons is indeed related to the presence of GABA. Both the myelinated and the unmyelinated regions of the GABA axons have higher neurofilament content and lower microtubule content compared to non-GABA axons.
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography analysis comparing myelinated and unmyelinated portions of the same axons

claim: Myelinated portions of GABA axons have higher neurofilament and lower microtubule content compared to the unmyelinated portions of the same axons.
source: There are also significant differences in cytoskeletal content between the different regions of GABA axons, where myelinated portions have higher neurofilament and lower microtubule content compared to the unmyelinated portions of the same axons.
evidence: This is a finding from array tomography analysis comparing myelinated and unmyelinated portions of the same axons

claim: The patchy distribution of myelin on basket cell axons is seemingly localized to the axon arbor near the cell body.
source: Our axon reconstructions showed that the distribution of myelin on basket cell axons is patchy and seemingly localized to the axon arbor near the cell body (e.g. Figures 3D–F, 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from volume EM and array tomography reconstructions

claim: The patchiness of myelin on basket cell axons qualitatively resembles the distribution of myelin on the descending axons of excitatory pyramidal cells.
source: This patchiness qualitatively resembles the distribution of myelin on the descending axons of excitatory pyramidal cells measured in the same EM data set (Tomassy et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from Tomassy et al., 2014

claim: The concentration of myelin on the proximal arbor is consistent with more complete reconstructions of individual filled cells in cat and macaque.
source: The concentration of myelin on the proximal arbor is also consistent with more complete reconstructions of individual filled cells in cat (Somogyi et al., 1983) and macaque (DeFelipe et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from Somogyi et al., 1983 and DeFelipe et al., 1986

claim: The fraction of somatic post-synaptic targets made by the inhibitory myelinated axons is at the low end of the previously reported range for cortical basket cells.
source: Consistent with the possibility that not all basket cells (or basket cell subtypes) are myelinated, the fraction of somatic post-synaptic targets made by the inhibitory myelinated axons described here is at the low end of the previously reported range for cortical basket cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison to literature values

claim: The majority of myelinated inhibitory axons contact dendritic shafts (53%) and spines (32%), and only 13% of the targets are cell bodies.
source: The majority of myelinated inhibitory axons in our study contact dendritic shafts (53%) and spines (32%), and only 13% of the targets are cell bodies.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from volume EM analysis

claim: The fraction of inhibitory post-synaptic targets made by the myelinated inhibitory axons (4.5%) is similar to, but somewhat lower than that previously observed in rat (8%) and cat (9%) neocortex.
source: The fraction of inhibitory post-synaptic targets made by the axons in this study (4.5%) is similar to, but somewhat lower than that previously observed in rat (8%) and cat (9%) neocortex (Somogyi et al., 1983; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from Somogyi et al., 1983 and Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998

claim: Nearly all cortical PV basket cells are fast-spiking.
source: Nearly all cortical PV basket cells are fast-spiking (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Galarreta and Hestrin, 1999, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Galarreta and Hestrin, 1999, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999

claim: Fast-spiking neurons have very high tonic activity compared to other cell types in cortex.
source: and fast-spiking neurons have very high tonic activity compared to other cell types in cortex (Gentet et al., 2010; Hofer et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gentet et al., 2010; Hofer et al., 2011

claim: Fast-spiking cells generate long trains of action potentials with very high frequency (>100 Hz).
source: — they generate long trains of action potentials with very high frequency (>100 Hz) (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Galarreta and Hestrin, 1999, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Galarreta and Hestrin, 1999, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999

claim: Fast-spiking cells exhibit a number of biophysical specializations that enable high firing rates but incur an increased energy cost per action potential.
source: Fast-spiking cells exhibit a number of biophysical specializations that enable high firing rates but incur an increased energy cost per action potential (Hu and Jonas, 2014; Carter and Bean, 2009; Hasenstaub et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu and Jonas, 2014; Carter and Bean, 2009; Hasenstaub et al., 2010

claim: Myelin is known to improve the energy efficiency of action potential propagation.
source: first, myelin is known to improve the energy efficiency of action potential propagation (Hartline and Colman, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hartline and Colman, 2007

claim: Myelin can provide metabolic support to the axon by supplying lactate as an energy source.
source: Secondly, myelin can provide metabolic support to the axon by supplying lactate as an energy source (Rinholm et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Morrison et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rinholm et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Morrison et al., 2013

claim: Myelin could reduce the basket cells' metabolic needs and provide an additional external energy supply from oligodendrocytes.
source: Thus, myelin could reduce the basket cells' metabolic needs and provide an additional external energy supply from oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known functions of myelin

claim: In young (~P30) mice, PV axon conduction velocities of ~0.5 m/s have been recorded.
source: No estimates of conduction velocities of cortical myelinated PV axons exist in the literature; however, in young (~P30) mice, PV axon conduction velocities of ~0.5 m/s have been recorded (Casale et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Casale et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014

claim: The majority of PV axons at P30 are most likely unmyelinated, since cortical myelination is not complete until much later (after P60).
source: The majority of PV axons at this age are most likely unmyelinated, since cortical myelination is not complete until much later (after P60) (Barrera et al., 2013; Mengler et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrera et al., 2013; Mengler et al., 2014

claim: An unmyelinated PV axon would conduct a spike in 0.4 ms to synapses located 200 μm away.
source: Using this conduction velocity estimate, an unmyelinated PV axon would conduct a spike in 0.4 ms to synapses located 200 μm away, which was the typical path length from cell body to proximal synapses in our EM-based reconstructions.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the conduction velocity estimate and measured path lengths

claim: Any reduction in the spike arrival time to proximal synapses due to myelination will inevitably be in the sub-millisecond range.
source: Thus, any reduction in the spike arrival time to proximal synapses due to myelination will inevitably be in the sub-millisecond range, likely too small a difference to affect post-synaptic dendritic integration or spike-timing-dependent plasticity, given the much slower timescales of those functions (Dan and Poo, 2006; Feldman, 2012; Stuart and Spruston, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculation and known timescales of synaptic functions, with supporting citations

claim: Spike time arrival differences on a sub-millisecond timescale might affect the magnitude of coordinated oscillations.
source: However, spike time arrival differences on a sub-millisecond timescale might affect the magnitude of coordinated oscillations (Pajevic et al., 2014), which are a known circuit role of basket cells.
evidence: This is a speculation with supporting citation to Pajevic et al., 2014

claim: Cortical myelin is dynamically remodeled during learning and development.
source: Cortical myelin is dynamically remodeled during learning and development (McKenzie et al., 2014; Bergles and Richardson, 2016; Makinodan et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to McKenzie et al., 2014; Bergles and Richardson, 2016; Makinodan et al., 2012

claim: Myelin redistributes during normal aging, where internode length decreases with age in primates.
source: and it redistributes during normal aging, where internode length decreases with age in primates (Peters, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peters, 2009

claim: MBP is one of the potential target antigens in MS.
source: Because MBP is one of the potential target antigens in MS (Wucherpfennig and Strominger, 1995; Fujinami and Oldstone, 1985; Garg and Smith, 2015), this finding has important implications for pathologies of myelin.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wucherpfennig and Strominger, 1995; Fujinami and Oldstone, 1985; Garg and Smith, 2015

claim: Gray matter myelin degeneration is observed in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease.
source: For example, gray matter myelin degeneration is observed in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Bartzokis, 2004; de la Monte, 1989)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartzokis, 2004; de la Monte, 1989

claim: In relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), the presence of cortical lesions is strongly correlated with seizure occurrence.
source: and, in relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), the presence of cortical lesions is strongly correlated with seizure occurrence (Calabrese et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calabrese et al., 2008

claim: Several diseases predicated on CNS demyelination, including neuromyelitis optica, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy may display seizure activity.
source: Several other diseases predicated on CNS demyelination, including neuromyelitis optica, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy may also display seizure activity (Jarius et al., 2014; Hynson et al., 2001; Lima et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jarius et al., 2014; Hynson et al., 2001; Lima et al., 2006

claim: Demyelination of PV interneurons may perturb the balance of large-network neuronal excitation and inhibition, biasing neocortical microcircuits toward seizure.
source: Demyelination of PV interneurons may perturb the balance of large-network neuronal excitation and inhibition, biasing neocortical microcircuits toward seizure.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential consequences of PV interneuron demyelination

claim: The ultrathin AT sections provide easy access of the antibodies against MBP and do not require lipid extraction.
source: The ultrathin AT sections provide easy access of the antibodies against MBP and do not require lipid extraction.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the advantages of the AT technique

claim: Immunofluorescence for MBP precisely outlines the myelinated sheaths of axons.
source: Conjugate light-electron AT confirms that immunofluorescence for MBP precisely outlines the myelinated sheaths of axons (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a validation finding from conjugate light-electron AT

claim: There is a strong correlation (R2=0.9) between myelin thickness measured from IF data and SEM data.
source: There is a strong correlation between the two measurements (R2=0.9), which allows the use of MBP immunofluorescence for more efficient sampling.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: In AT experiments, GABA and PV immunostaining within axons is not affected by myelination.
source: In addition, the use of ultrathin sections ensures that antigens can be detected equally well within myelinated and unmyelinated portions of the axon. For example, in our AT experiments GABA and PV immunostaining within axons is not affected by myelination (Figures 1, 3)
evidence: This is a methodological validation finding

claim: In preembedding immunocytochemistry, myelinated portions of axons are much more weakly stained than unmyelinated portions.
source: in contrast to preembedding immunocytochemistry where myelinated portions of axons are much more weakly stained (Pawelzik et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pawelzik et al., 2002

claim: The number of MBP profiles dramatically increases with cortical depth.

claim: About half of cortical GABA neurons contain parvalbumin.
source: Cortical GABA neurons are a highly diverse population (Ascoli et al., 2008; Markram et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2010). About half of them contain parvalbumin (PV), a calcium buffering protein.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with supporting citations

claim: Parvalbumin is found in basket cells, chandelier cells, and in a sparse sub-population of long-range inhibitory axons arising from basal forebrain.
source: Among the inhibitory neurons of cortex, parvalbumin is found in basket cells, chandelier cells (Markram et al., 2004; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; DeFelipe et al., 1989), and in a sparse sub-population of long-range inhibitory axons arising from basal forebrain (Freund and Gulyás, 1991; Caputi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Markram et al., 2004; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; DeFelipe et al., 1989; Freund and Gulyás, 1991; Caputi et al., 2013

claim: Chandelier cells have an axonal arbor which resembles a chandelier, with vertically oriented axonal cartridges that almost exclusively form synapses onto the axon initial segments of pyramidal neurons.
source: Chandelier cells have an axonal arbor which resembles a chandelier, with vertically oriented axonal cartridges that almost exclusively form synapses onto the axon initial segments of pyramidal neurons (Somogyi et al., 1982).

claim: A large (but variable) fraction of basket cell synapses are with dendritic shafts and spines.

evidence: Supported by citations to Somogyi et al., 1983; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998; Kisvarday et al., 1987; Tamás et al., 1997

claim: The majority of basket cells originate from PV interneurons.
source: Thus, we conclude that the majority of myelinated inhibitory axons belong to the intracortical axons of parvalbumin containing basket cells.
